name: Quantum Supremacy Defined
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: A Narrow Claim That Got a Very Big Headline
lesson.summary: Quantum supremacy means a quantum computer beat the best classical computer at some specific task, not that the task was useful, and the definition's narrowness is exactly where the hype gets ahead of the substance.
lesson.body:
Once you have heard about what quantum computers could supposedly do, from breaking encryption to searching enormous datasets, the natural next question is whether anyone has actually shown a quantum computer beating a classical one at anything at all. That is precisely what the term quantum supremacy was coined to describe, and its formal definition is much narrower than the headlines built around it suggest: quantum supremacy means a quantum computer has performed some specific, well defined computational task faster than the best available classical computer or algorithm could perform that same task, full stop. It says nothing about whether the task is useful, only that it was hard for a classical machine and easy for a quantum one.

The most famous claim came from Google in 2019, using a 53 qubit superconducting processor called Sycamore. The task was random circuit sampling: running a specific, essentially arbitrary sequence of quantum gates and sampling from the resulting probability distribution of outputs, something straightforward for the quantum device to do physically but, according to the original claim, expected to take a classical supercomputer on the order of ten thousand years to simulate, compared to roughly two hundred seconds on the quantum processor. That comparison was the basis for declaring quantum supremacy achieved.

It was also immediately and productively contested. IBM researchers argued that a better classical simulation strategy, using more disk storage and smarter algorithms, could bring the classical time down to a few days rather than ten thousand years, and subsequent academic work pushed classical simulation techniques further still, continuing to narrow the gap in the years since. This back and forth is not a scandal, it is exactly how the field is supposed to work: a quantum supremacy claim is inherently a claim about the current best classical algorithm, and classical algorithms keep improving, which means any specific supremacy claim has a shelf life and needs revisiting as classical methods catch up.

The deeper point worth holding onto is that random circuit sampling, and similar tasks like the boson sampling experiments run on photonic hardware, were chosen specifically because they are hard to simulate classically, not because anyone needs the output for anything. Winning at a task engineered to be a bad fit for classical computers is a meaningful scientific milestone, it demonstrates real quantum control at a scale that matters, but it is not the same claim as a quantum computer being useful for a real world problem. That distinction, between beating a classical computer at an artificial task and beating one at a task anyone actually cares about, is exactly what the next chapter's concept, quantum advantage, tries to separate out.
